questions.stem: An annuity is an investment in which:
options: equal contributions are made regularly and interest compounds each period
a single sum is invested once and earns simple interest for a fixed term
a single sum is invested once and earns compound interest for a fixed term
equal contributions are made regularly but no interest is earned on them
questions.explanation: An annuity involves regular, equal payments with interest compounding at the end of each period. A single sum earning compound interest is an ordinary compound interest investment, not an annuity.

questions.stem: Which of these is also an annuity?
options: A single sum invested, from which equal regular withdrawals are made
A single sum invested in a term deposit until the end of its term
A share portfolio that pays dividends twice a year to its owner
A savings account into which money is deposited only occasionally
questions.explanation: An annuity can work in either direction: regular equal contributions build up a sum, or a sum is invested and regular equal withdrawals are paid out of it, as in a retirement income stream.

questions.stem: Superannuation is an example of an annuity because:
options: the money earns simple interest until the person retires from work
the person can withdraw any amount at any time before they retire
regular contributions are made and interest compounds over many years
one large contribution is made when a person first starts working
questions.explanation: Employers and employees make regular contributions into a super fund, which earns compound returns until retirement. Super cannot usually be withdrawn before retirement age.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an annuity and a compound interest investment?
options: An annuity earns no interest; the other earns compound interest each period
An annuity has regular contributions; compound interest has one sum invested
An annuity earns compound interest; the other earns simple interest instead
An annuity has one sum invested; compound interest has regular contributions
questions.explanation: Both earn compound interest. In a compound interest investment one present value grows, while an annuity also adds equal contributions every period.

questions.stem: The present value of an annuity is:
options: the interest earned by the annuity over the whole of its term
the single sum invested now that would grow to the same future value
the total of all the contributions made over the term of the annuity
the value of the annuity at the end of its final contribution period
questions.explanation: The present value is the lump sum that, invested now at the same rate, would be worth the same as the annuity at the end. The value at the end is the future value.

questions.stem: A retiree's fund pays $3000 at the end of each month until the money runs out. This is an annuity in which:
options: equal regular contributions are made and the balance keeps growing
the balance stays the same, because only the interest is withdrawn
each withdrawal is larger than the one that was made before it
a single sum is invested and equal regular withdrawals are made
questions.explanation: A sum is invested and equal amounts are withdrawn each month, while the remaining balance earns interest, until the balance reaches zero. If only the interest were withdrawn, the money would never run out.

questions.stem: $1000 is deposited at the end of each year into an account earning 5% p.a. compounded annually. What is the balance at the end of year 2, just after the second deposit?
questions.explanation: Year 1 ends with $1000 (no interest yet, because the deposit is made at the end of the year). In year 2 the $1000 earns $50 interest, and the second deposit is added: 1000 + 50 + 1000 = $2050. $2152.50 treats the deposits as made at the start of each year.

questions.stem: $1000 is deposited at the end of each year into an account earning 5% p.a. compounded annually. The balance is $2050 after 2 years. How much interest is earned in year 3?
questions.explanation: Interest in year 3 is 5% of the opening balance of $2050, which is $102.50. $150 is 5% of $3000, which wrongly includes the year 3 deposit before it is made.

questions.stem: $1000 is deposited at the end of each year into an account earning 5% p.a. compounded annually. What is the balance at the end of year 3, just after the third deposit?
questions.explanation: End of year 2: $2050. Year 3: interest 0.05 × 2050 = $102.50, so the balance is 2050 + 102.50 + 1000 = $3152.50. $3150.00 takes 5% of the total deposited instead of 5% of the balance at the start of the year.

questions.stem: A retiree invests $10 000 at 4% p.a. compounded annually and withdraws $2500 at the end of each year. What is the balance after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Year 1: 10 000 + 400 − 2500 = $7900. Year 2: 7900 + 316 − 2500 = $5716. $5800 charges $400 interest in both years, ignoring the smaller balance in year 2, and $5512 takes each withdrawal out before adding the interest.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, column B holds the balance of an annuity at the end of each year. Interest is 5% p.a. and $1000 is deposited at the end of each year. Which formula in B3 calculates the next balance from B2?
questions.explanation: Each year the previous balance earns 5% interest (multiply by 1.05) and then the deposit of $1000 is added. =B2*1.05 leaves out the deposit, and =B2+1000*1.05 gives interest to the new deposit instead of the balance.

questions.stem: To find the future value of an annuity from a table of future value interest factors, you:
options: multiply the total of all contributions by the factor
add the factor to the total of all the contributions
multiply the contribution per period by the factor
divide the contribution per period by the factor
questions.explanation: Future value = contribution per period × future value interest factor for the rate per period r and the number of periods n. Multiplying the total of the contributions by the factor counts every payment many times over.

questions.stem: In a table of future value interest factors for annuities, the factor for 1 period is 1 at every interest rate. Why?
options: The single contribution is made at the end and earns no interest
The interest for one period is too small to be shown in the table
Interest is not paid on an annuity until the second period begins
A one-period annuity earns simple interest instead of compound
questions.explanation: With one period, the only contribution is made at the end of that period, so it has had no time to earn interest and the future value equals the contribution.

questions.stem: $200 is invested at the end of each month for 5 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. The future value interest factor for r = 0.5% and n = 60 is 69.7700. What is the future value?
questions.explanation: Monthly rate 6% ÷ 12 = 0.5%, and 5 × 12 = 60 periods. FV = 200 × 69.7700 = $13 954.00. $12 000 is the contributions without interest, and $1127.42 uses the yearly factor with monthly payments.

questions.stem: $200 is invested at the end of each month for 5 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly, giving a future value of $13 954.00. How much interest is earned?
questions.explanation: The contributions total 200 × 60 = $12 000, so the interest is 13 954.00 − 12 000 = $1954.00. $12 000 is the total contributed, and $837.24 is 6% of $13 954, which is not how annuity interest is found.

questions.stem: A person wants $50 000 in 8 years. They will make equal deposits at the end of each year into an account earning 5% p.a. compounded annually. The future value interest factor for r = 5% and n = 8 is 9.5491. What deposit is needed each year?
questions.explanation: Contribution = FV ÷ factor = 50 000 ÷ 9.5491 = $5236.10. $6250 is 50 000 ÷ 8, which ignores interest, and $477 455 multiplies by the factor instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A fund earning 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly will pay $1500 at the end of each month for 10 years. The present value interest factor for r = 0.4% and n = 120 is 95.1560. How much must be in the fund at the start?
questions.explanation: Present value = withdrawal × present value interest factor = 1500 × 95.1560 = $142 734.00. $180 000 is the total of all the withdrawals, but interest is earned on the money left in the fund. $230 447.94 uses a future value factor instead of a present value factor.

questions.stem: An annuity of $200 per month for 60 months at 0.5% per month has a future value of $13 954.00. The present value interest factor for r = 0.5% and n = 60 is 51.7256. What single sum, invested now at the same rate, would have the same future value?
questions.explanation: The single sum is the present value of the annuity: 200 × 51.7256 = $10 345.12. Invested now at 0.5% per month for 60 months, it grows to about $13 954. $12 000 is just the total of the contributions.

questions.stem: In a table of future value interest factors, what happens to the factor as the interest rate increases for the same number of periods?
options: It decreases
It stays the same
It halves
It increases
questions.explanation: A higher rate means each contribution earns more interest, so the future value of each dollar contributed, and hence the factor, increases.

questions.stem: In a table of present value interest factors, what happens to the factor as the interest rate increases for the same number of periods?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It doubles
questions.explanation: At a higher rate, a smaller starting sum is needed to fund the same withdrawals, because more interest is earned on the balance. So the present value factor decreases as the rate rises.

questions.stem: A person makes equal monthly deposits of $500 into an account earning 1% per month. Future value interest factors at r = 1% are 26.9735 for n = 24, 43.0769 for n = 36 and 61.2226 for n = 48. Which is the shortest of these terms that reaches $20 000?
options: 48 months
40 months
36 months
24 months
questions.explanation: 500 × 26.9735 = $13 486.75 after 24 months, which is too little, and 500 × 43.0769 = $21 538.45 after 36 months, which is enough. 40 months is not a term given in the table.

questions.stem: Which change increases the future value of an annuity, with everything else kept the same?
options: Making fewer contributions in total
Increasing the regular contribution
Decreasing the interest rate
Shortening the term of the annuity
questions.explanation: A larger contribution increases the future value in proportion. A lower rate, a shorter term or fewer contributions all reduce it.

questions.stem: At 5% p.a. compounded annually, the future value interest factors are 12.5779 for n = 10 and 5.5256 for n = 5. Ana saves $1000 a year for 10 years; Ben saves $2000 a year for 5 years, and both finish saving at the same time. Both deposit $10 000 in total. Who ends with more, and why?
options: Neither, because both deposit the same total of $10 000
Ben, because his money is invested for fewer years
Ana, because her early deposits earn interest for longer
Ben, because his deposits each year are twice as large
questions.explanation: Ana: 1000 × 12.5779 = $12 577.90. Ben: 2000 × 5.5256 = $11 051.20. Ana's money is invested over 10 years, so her early deposits earn compound interest for longer.

questions.stem: Two people each contribute $300 a month to an annuity at the same interest rate. One starts at age 25 and the other at 35, and both stop at 65. Compared with the later starter, the earlier starter will have:
options: the same, because both make contributions at the same rate each month
less, because money invested for longer earns a lower rate of interest
much more, because extra years of compounding increase the value greatly
exactly $36 000 more, the extra ten years of contributions without interest
questions.explanation: The early starter makes 120 more contributions, and all of the money compounds for longer, so the difference is far more than the extra $36 000 contributed. This is why starting superannuation early matters.

questions.stem: Increasing the interest rate of an annuity has a greater effect on its future value when:
options: the term is short, because the interest has less time to be added on
the contributions are small, because interest is a percentage of them
the contributions are made less often, so that each one is larger
the term is long, because the extra interest compounds over more periods
questions.explanation: The benefit of a higher rate compounds, so over a long term it builds into a much larger difference in future value. Over a short term there is little time for the extra interest to grow.

questions.stem: A worker's superannuation receives $500 at the end of each month for 30 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. The future value interest factor for r = 0.5% and n = 360 is 1004.5150. What is the final value?
questions.explanation: FV = 500 × 1004.5150 = $502 257.50. The contributions alone are 500 × 360 = $180 000, so most of the final value is interest. $39 529.10 uses a yearly factor for monthly contributions.

questions.stem: A worker's superannuation receives $500 at the end of each month for 30 years and grows to $502 257.50. How much of the final value is interest?
questions.explanation: Contributions = 500 × 12 × 30 = $180 000. Interest = 502 257.50 − 180 000 = $322 257.50. The final value includes the contributions, so it is not all interest.

questions.stem: A loan is repaid by equal monthly repayments, and its amount is the present value of those repayments. Repayments of $2000 a month for 25 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly have a present value interest factor of 155.2069. What is the largest amount that can be borrowed?
questions.explanation: Loan = repayment × present value factor = 2000 × 155.2069 = $310 413.80. $600 000 is the total of all repayments, which includes interest on the loan.

questions.stem: $300 000 is borrowed for 25 years at 6% p.a. compounded monthly. The present value interest factor for r = 0.5% and n = 300 is 155.2069. What is the monthly repayment?
questions.explanation: Repayment = loan ÷ present value factor = 300 000 ÷ 155.2069 = $1932.90. $1000 is 300 000 ÷ 300, which ignores interest, and $1500 is only the first month's interest, so the balance would never fall.

questions.stem: A $300 000 loan is repaid with 300 monthly repayments of $1932.90. How much interest is paid over the life of the loan?
questions.explanation: Total repaid = 300 × 1932.90 = $579 870.00, so interest = 579 870 − 300 000 = $279 870.00. $579 870 is the total repaid, not just the interest.

questions.stem: For a loan repaid by equal regular repayments, the amount borrowed is found from:
options: the total of the repayments
the first repayment times the rate
the present value of the repayments
the future value of the repayments
questions.explanation: The amount borrowed today is the present value of all the future repayments. The total of the repayments is larger, because it includes the interest.

questions.stem: A savings plan makes deposits of $100 at the end of each week. The interest rate is 5.2% p.a. compounded weekly. What interest rate per period and number of periods are used for 3 years?
options: r = 5.2% and n = 3
questions.explanation: Weekly rate = 5.2% ÷ 52 = 0.1%, and there are 3 × 52 = 156 weeks. Using 36 treats the term as monthly, and using 5.2% with weekly periods applies the yearly rate every week.

questions.stem: A person can either deposit a single sum now or make equal yearly deposits of $3000 for 6 years, at 4% p.a. compounded annually. The present value interest factor for r = 4% and n = 6 is 5.2421. What single sum gives the same final value as the yearly deposits?
questions.explanation: The equivalent single sum is the present value of the annuity: 3000 × 5.2421 = $15 726.30. $18 000 is the total of the deposits, which ignores the interest the single sum would earn over 6 years.

questions.stem: In the standard tables of annuity interest factors, each contribution is assumed to be made:
options: halfway through each period
at the end of each period
at the start of each period
only at the end of the term
questions.explanation: The standard tables assume each contribution or withdrawal is made at the end of each period, just after interest is calculated. This is why the factor for one period is 1.

questions.stem: A future value interest factor table has the factor for r = 1% and n = 10 as 10.4622 and for r = 2% and n = 10 as 10.9497. Contributions of $1000 are made each period for 10 periods. How much more is the future value at 2% than at 1%?
questions.explanation: At 2%: 1000 × 10.9497 = $10 949.70. At 1%: 1000 × 10.4622 = $10 462.20. The difference is $487.50. Doubling the rate does not double the future value.

questions.stem: A retiree wants to withdraw $1500 a month for 10 years from a fund earning 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly, and needs $142 734 at the start. Which change would reduce the amount needed at the start?
options: A longer period of withdrawals
Larger monthly withdrawals
Withdrawals made each week instead
A higher interest rate on the fund
questions.explanation: A higher rate means the money left in the fund earns more, so less is needed at the start. A longer period or larger withdrawals need more money, and weekly withdrawals of the same monthly total change little.

questions.stem: Over 4 years, $1000 deposited at the end of each year at 5% p.a. gives a future value of $4310.13. A one-off deposit of $4000 at the start, at the same rate, grows to $4862.03. Why is the one-off deposit worth more?
options: All of it earns interest for the full 4 years
It earns a higher interest rate than the annuity
It is compounded more often than the annuity is
More money is deposited altogether than in the annuity
questions.explanation: Both deposit $4000 in total at the same rate, but the lump sum earns interest for all 4 years, while the annuity's deposits are spread out and the last one earns no interest at all.
